name: Democratic socialism
summary: Democratic socialism seeks democratic control of economic life alongside competitive political democracy, civil liberties and social equality. Its defining accounts extend democracy to workplaces and combine social ownership with universal social protection, while differing about markets and the pace of transformation. The tradition also sets out international cooperation and opposition to imperialism; specific policies of socialist organisations are not automatically its tenets.
scope: Democratic socialism as defined in Busky, Democratic Socialism: A Global Survey (introduction and available chapter 1, especially pp. 7–12), the Oxford World Encyclopedia entry and the democratic-socialist passages of SEP, together with explicit self-definitions: the Socialist International’s Aims and Tasks of Democratic Socialism (1951), its 1989 Declaration’s account of the ideology’s principles and economic democracy, and Neal Meyer’s What Is Democratic Socialism? (2018), and DSA North Star’s expressly labelled vision of democratic socialism (Statement of Principles, updated 2023). These sources describe a diverse democratic socialist tradition, including disagreements about markets, ownership forms and speed of change. An organisation’s or author’s definition counts only for the tenets it attributes to democratic socialism; present-day candidate endorsements, campaign lists, SI-specific policy demands and the wider platforms or records of member parties do not. No individual thinker’s complete body of work is imported. Newman and Sears remain only as evidence of replaced answers in reviewHistory; their supplied books were located and checked in the reference corpus, but their general accounts of socialism do not add specific democratic-socialist tenets.

notes: Test pass authorised by the maintainer before the normal re-audit gap: removal of the family-only restriction. All statements were checked literally, including candidates. Searched economy, government and liberty in the complete 1951 and 1989 declarations; society/culture in their rights, equality and cultural sections; world/globalism in international democracy and North–South sections; means in Busky and Meyer; ecology and technology in the declarations, Busky’s introduction and targeted searches. General environmental stewardship does not settle nuclear power, climate science, growth limits or animal rights. Freedom of religion does not settle apostasy or blasphemy laws under the explicit general-value rule. Cultural autonomy does not choose territorial autonomy, school-language policy or statehood. No official-doctrine state record is established here; member-party government is not the ideology’s own record. DSA definition and sustainability pages, Harrington’s archived essay, Chatham House’s introduction and Newman’s publisher page returned 403 and were not retried. Available publisher preview of Busky ends during chapter 1; no claim is made to have read unavailable chapters. The maintainer-supplied Newman and Sears books were subsequently located in the external reference corpus and searched across themes; Newman does not name democratic socialism, and Sears’s references to it do not establish further tenets. Their complete supplied texts are saved in the source library; their evidence remains in signed historical versions, not current answers. Targeted follow-up searches covered civil liberties and religion, nuclear disarmament, ecology and technology; North Star’s explicit definitions were read in full. Its views on current elections, closing particular bases, US Senate abolition and internal organisational procedures were not imported. Rights to reproductive freedom do not specify abortion’s legal scope here; environmental responsibility does not by itself choose growth limits, nuclear power or a particular climate policy. Natural resources as common property does settle the existing resource-ownership statement, but does not decide national versus foreign ownership. No aliases or defining authors were added: references to social democracy as another usage do not justify aliasing two separately catalogued ideologies.
